audience.programmeDescription: Twente’s English-taught Civil Engineering degree starts with construction, water and transport. Students then apply engineering methods to delta safety, sustainable construction, area development and simulation. The third year includes a minor and a graduation semester.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options explore water risks or infrastructure impacts through environmental science, quantitative methods, ecology and governance. Twente’s programme develops civil engineering design and requires a supervised thesis in the field.

curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC curriculum includes 30 EC of minor study and a 30 EC graduation semester.

componentNotes.ce-y3-minor: Students choose an approved 30 EC minor, subject to entry requirements.
componentNotes.ce-y3-preparation: Graduation normally follows completion of modules 1–8. The preparation quarter leads into the final assignment.
componentNotes.ce-y3-thesis: The 15 EC assignment is normally carried out with a civil engineering company or institution.

notes.text: The UCR options share some mathematics, water management and sustainability methods with Twente. Twente builds a separate sequence in structures, hydraulics, geotechnics, transport and construction design, with integrated engineering projects.

ENSGATE101.text: Introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries and scientific tools for understanding human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and study chemical and physical principles relevant to climate, energy and materials. A laboratory project makes and tests starch-based biopolymers.

ENSSUST313.text: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
